newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australians more uncertain about becoming republic.
newsitem.headline: Australians more uncertain about becoming republic.

text.p: More and more Australians are having a hard time deciding if they want their country to become a republic or remain a constitutional monarchy, according to a newspaper poll published on Thursday.
One in four Australians cannot decide on the issue -- by far the highest number in the past decade, the poll in The Australian national daily said.

The poll found 47 percent of those surveyed backed a republic and 28 percent wanted to remain a constitutional monarchy with Britain's Queen Elizabeth as head-of-state. A constitutional convention on the issue is due later this year.
But both numbers were down on the last survey, in June 1995, with pro-republican sentiment falling from 50 percent and the number of monarchists dropping from 35 percent.
The uncommitted number jumped to 25 percent from 15 percent and is well above the previous peak of 19 percent -- in early 1993 and again early 1995 -- since the paper began republic polls in 1987.
The public push for a republic has slowed since conservative Prime Minister John Howard, an avowed monarchist, ousted republican Labor prime minister Paul Keating in a national election a year ago.
Howard this month said he would hold a national convention to examine constitutional issues late this year, before considering a popular vote on becoming a republic.

Howard has acknowledged a desire for change among a substantial part of the Australian community, but says the country's economic problems will receive top priority from his Liberal-National government.
The Australian's poll surveyed 1,200 voters around the country from February 7 to 9.
